enhanced_information: In drug-induced hemolytic anemia, red blood cell destruction leads to the release of intracellular enzymes. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a well-established marker for hemolysis because it is released from lysed red blood cells, leading to elevated LDH levels in the blood. This aligns with the evidence path showing the interaction of erythrocytes with lactate dehydrogenase. Aspartate aminotransferase (AST) can also be elevated due to hemolysis, but it is less specific than LDH. Creatine kinase (CK) is primarily associated with muscle damage and is not typically elevated in hemolytic anemia. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) deficiency can cause hemolytic anemia, but G6PDH levels themselves are not elevated during hemolysis; rather, a deficiency in G6PDH can predispose individuals to hemolysis. Therefore, lactate dehydrogenase is the most appropriate marker for drug-induced hemolytic anemia.
analysis: In drug-induced hemolytic anemia, the destruction of red blood cells leads to the release of intracellular enzymes. Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is a well-established marker for hemolysis because it is released from lysed red blood cells, resulting in elevated LDH levels in the blood. This makes LDH a specific and reliable marker for hemolysis. While aspartate aminotransferase (AST) can also be elevated due to hemolysis, it is less specific than LDH. Creatine kinase (CK) is primarily associated with muscle damage and is not typically elevated in hemolytic anemia. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PDH) deficiency can cause hemolytic anemia, but G6PDH levels themselves are not elevated during hemolysis; rather, a deficiency in G6PDH can predispose individuals to hemolysis. Therefore, based on standard medical knowledge and consensus, lactate dehydrogenase is the most appropriate marker for drug-induced hemolytic anemia.
